warmup.q: fun items(): Flow<Item> = flow { println("fetching"); emit(shop.firstPage()) }. You call val f = items() and then f.collect { } twice. How many times does fetching print?
options: Once, at the first collect; the second one reuses the values
Twice: the body runs again for every collector
Never: println inside a flow builder is ignored
warmup.why: A flow { } is cold, like a recipe card. Calling items() only writes the card, and the body runs from the top each time someone collects it. Nothing is kept between collectors, which is also why a retry can simply collect again.

opening:
A recipe card is a quiet thing. Writing one cooks nothing: the card for lemon cake can sit in a drawer for a year, and the kitchen stays clean. Only when somebody cooks from it does anything happen, from the top, one step at a time. If two people cook from the same card on the same day, every step happens twice, and two cakes come out.

So far, each coroutine in this track gave back one value at most, like the one pot of sauce from async, and the last lesson asked how code can hand back many. Kotlin's answer is Flow, a stream of values such as the items of a shop's aisle or the lines of a delivery note, and it behaves like the recipe card. The easy trap is to think that building a flow starts the work, or that a second reader shares the first one's results.

In this lesson, we'll write a flow, watch it run once per reader, add steps to it, move its slow part elsewhere, and handle its errors in the right place. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a recipe card that cooks nothing until somebody cooks from it. A cold flow is that card. Building it and adding steps runs nothing, each collector runs it from the top, and flowOn and catch both act on the steps above them.

Now look in your own code for a suspend fun that returns a List built with toList(). It may want to return a Flow instead. And check that every .catch sits below the steps it should cover.

Next, we'll hang a board in the hall that always shows today's menu. What does a flow look like when it runs whether anyone watches or not, and how do many collectors share one run?

sections.h: A flow is a recipe card that runs once per collector
sections.html:
A flow is a stream of values that you receive one at a time, through a suspend call. (A suspend function is one that can pause without holding its thread, the worker that runs the code.) The usual way to make one is the flow { } builder, a block in which you call emit once for each value.

Here's a flow of the items in one aisle of a grocer's online shop. The shop's website lists an aisle a page at a time. You ask for the first page, and each page carries a cursor, a small bookmark that says where the next page starts:

Java
// Java equivalent: a cold Reactor Flux that asks for the next page once the previous one is in
Flux<Item> aisleItems(GroceryShop shop, String aisle) {
    return shop.page(aisle, null)                                        // Mono<ItemPage>
        .expand(p -> p.nextCursor() == null ? Mono.empty() : shop.page(aisle, p.nextCursor()))
        .flatMapIterable(ItemPage::items);
}
Kotlin
fun aisleItems(shop: GroceryShop, aisle: String): Flow<Item> = flow {
    var cursor: String? = null
    do {
        val page = shop.page(aisle, cursor)   // a suspend call to the shop's website
        for (item in page.items) emit(item)
        cursor = page.nextCursor
    } while (cursor != null)
}

Calling aisleItems(...) runs nothing. It returns the recipe card, a description of the work. The body runs when someone calls a terminal operator, a suspend function such as collect or toList that reads the flow to the end. It runs again from the top for every collector, every caller doing that reading. A flow that behaves this way is cold. A Reactor Flux, from the reactive track, is cold in the same way: nothing happens until you subscribe.

ColdFlow, in the Try it below, checks those claims on a smaller aisle, with two items on each of three pages. It builds the flow, collects it twice, then takes three items. Predict every fetching line first:

building the flow
built; nothing fetched yet
first collect:
  fetching page 0 of the fruit aisle
  fetching page 1 of the fruit aisle
  fetching page 2 of the fruit aisle
  got [apples, bananas, cherries, dates, figs, grapes]
second collect:
  fetching page 0 of the fruit aisle
  fetching page 1 of the fruit aisle
  fetching page 2 of the fruit aisle
  got [apples, bananas, cherries, dates, figs, grapes]
take(3):
  fetching page 0 of the fruit aisle
  fetching page 1 of the fruit aisle
  got [apples, bananas, cherries]

Building printed nothing. Each collection fetched all three pages again. And take(3) stopped after page 1, because the third item was on it. The figs and grapes were never fetched, because nobody asked for them.

Two properties explain that last line. First, a flow is sequential: emit is a suspend call that returns only when the collector has finished with the value, so the producer never runs ahead of the consumer. That's Flow's backpressure, the way a slow consumer slows the producer down, with no request(n) from the reactive track in sight. Second, a collector that stops early stops the producer. take(3) cancels the flow after the third value, the cancel from Cancellation and timeouts, so the loop never asks for page 2.

The other builders are shortcuts. flowOf(a, b, c) emits fixed values, and list.asFlow() or (1..n).asFlow() turn collections and ranges into flows. One caution: flow { } checks for cancellation at every emit, but asFlow() doesn't, so add .cancellable() to a long one that must stop on time. channelFlow and callbackFlow are for producers that aren't plain step-by-step code, and lesson 9 of this track covers them.

Here the recipe picture breaks. Two cooks with one card make two cakes, and a real kitchen would notice the waste. A cold flow doesn't: three collectors fetch every page three times, and nothing warns you. Sharing one run is lesson 8 of this track.

Building a flow runs nothing. Each collector runs it again, from the top.

The card has one step so far: emit each item. Real recipes have more steps, and so do flows.

code.title: ColdFlow.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.take import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.toList import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking private val pages = listOf(listOf("apples", "bananas"), listOf("cherries", "dates"), listOf("figs", "grapes")) /** Three pages of two items each, from the grocer's shop, which takes 20 ms per page. */ fun aisle(name: String): Flow<String> = flow { for ((page, items) in pages.withIndex()) { println(" fetching page $page of the $name aisle") delay(20) for (item in items) emit(item) } } fun main() = runBlocking { println("building the flow") val fruit = aisle("fruit") println("built; nothing fetched yet") println("first collect:") println(" got ${fruit.toList()}") println("second collect:") println(" got ${fruit.toList()}") println("take(3):") println(" got ${fruit.take(3).toList()}") }

alt.title: ColdFlowJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of ColdFlow.kt: a Reactor Flux is cold too. Nothing runs until you subscribe, // every subscription starts again, and take(3) cancels the source when it has enough. package workbench.coroutines.l07; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; public class ColdFlowJava { static final List<List<String>> PAGES = List.of(List.of("apples", "bananas"), List.of("cherries", "dates"), List.of("figs", "grapes")); static Flux<String> aisle(String name) { return Flux.range(0, 3) .concatMap(page -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> { System.out.println(" fetching page " + page + " of the " + name + " aisle"); return PAGES.get(page); }).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(20)), 1) // prefetch 1: ask for one page at a time .flatMapIterable(items -> items); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("building the flux"); Flux<String> fruit = aisle("fruit"); System.out.println("built; nothing fetched yet"); System.out.println("first subscribe:"); System.out.println(" got " + fruit.collectList().block()); System.out.println("second subscribe:"); System.out.println(" got " + fruit.collectList().block()); System.out.println("take(3):"); System.out.println(" got " + fruit.take(3).collectList().block()); } }

try.expect: Building prints nothing. Each full collection fetches pages 0, 1 and 2 again. take(3) fetches pages 0 and 1, because the third item, cherries, is on page 1, and the flow is cancelled before page 2. With take(2) only page 0 is fetched. The Java twin prints the same lines, because a Flux is cold too.

aside.title: Isn't this just a Sequence?
aside.html: Close, but not quite. A Kotlin Sequence is lazy too, and it also runs its steps once per iteration, one value at a time. The difference is waiting. The block of sequence { } can call yield, but it can't call a suspend function such as delay or a page fetch, so a Sequence that waits has to block its thread. A flow's builder and steps are suspend code, so they wait without holding a thread, and a cancel can reach them. Use a Sequence for work that never waits, and a Flow when some step does.

video.title: A cold flow is a recipe card: it cooks nothing until someone collects, and each collector cooks it from the top; steps only write on the card, the terminal one cooks, flowOn moves the steps above it, catch handles what falls from above and onCompletion every ending

sections.h: Steps on the card: intermediate operators build, terminal operators run
sections.html:
Operators are the steps written on the card: wash, peel, chop. They come in two kinds. Intermediate operators such as map, filter, onEach, take and transform take a flow and return a new flow. They're plain functions: they return at once and run nothing, like writing one more line on the card. Terminal operators such as collect, toList, first, fold and count are suspend functions. They start the flow, read it, and return when it ends. That's somebody cooking.

Java
// Java equivalent: Reactor operators also only build; block() (or subscribe) runs them
Flux<String> bargains = aisleItems(shop, "fruit")
    .filter(i -> i.priceCents() < 200)
    .map(i -> String.format("%s: %.2f", i.name(), i.priceCents() / 100.0));
List<String> firstTen = bargains.take(10).collectList().block();
Kotlin
val bargains: Flow<String> = aisleItems(shop, "fruit")    // nothing runs yet
    .filter { it.priceCents < 200 }
    .map { "${it.name}: %.2f".format(it.priceCents / 100.0) }
val firstTen = bargains.take(10).toList()                 // now it runs

By default all of it runs in one coroutine, one value at a time. Predict the order in which these lines print. OperatorOrder, in the Try it below, sends three weights from the kitchen scale through a filter and a map, and prints at every step. (A negative reading means the scale wasn't set to zero.)

pipeline built: no line above has printed yet
emit    250
  filter passed 250
    map   -> 0.25 kg
      collect 0.25 kg
emit    -40
emit    1200
  filter passed 1200
    map   -> 1.20 kg
      collect 1.20 kg

The first weight went all the way into the collector before the second one was even emitted, and the -40 stopped at the filter. There are no queues between the steps and no extra threads. Each emit, in the end, is a plain call into the next step's code. The few operators that add concurrency on purpose, such as buffer, flowOn and flatMapMerge, say so in their docs.

A reusable step is just an extension function, and it reads like a built-in one:

Java
// Java equivalent: a function from Flux to Flux, applied with transform
static Function<Flux<Item>, Flux<Item>> under(long cents) {
    return items -> items.filter(i -> i.priceCents() < cents);
}

Flux<Item> cheapFruit = aisleItems(shop, "fruit").transform(under(200));
Kotlin
fun Flow<Item>.under(cents: Long): Flow<Item> = filter { it.priceCents < cents }

val cheapFruit = aisleItems(shop, "fruit").under(200)

transform { value -> ... } is the general form: it can emit zero, one or many values for each value that comes in.

Watch for a terminal operator hiding in a function that ought to return a flow. suspend fun bargains(): List<String> = pipeline.toList() cooks the whole recipe at the call and holds every line in memory. fun bargains(): Flow<String> leaves the caller free to stream it, take the first ten, or stop early.

Intermediate operators only write steps on the card. A terminal operator cooks.

Every step so far ran on the collector's thread. That's fine for a filter. It isn't fine when one of the steps blocks.

try.title: Watch one value at a time

Run it.

code.title: OperatorOrder.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.filter import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOf import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.onEach import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking fun main() = runBlocking { // weights in grams from the kitchen scale; a negative reading means it wasn't set to zero val pipeline = flowOf(250L, -40L, 1_200L) .onEach { println("emit $it") } .filter { it > 0 }.onEach { println(" filter passed $it") } .map { "%.2f kg".format(it / 1_000.0) }.onEach { println(" map -> $it") } println("pipeline built: no line above has printed yet") pipeline.collect { println(" collect $it") } }

alt.title: OperatorOrderJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of OperatorOrder.kt: a synchronous Flux also moves one item through the whole // chain before the source produces the next one, and nothing runs until subscribe(). package workbench.coroutines.l07; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; public class OperatorOrderJava { public static void main(String[] args) { // weights in grams from the kitchen scale; a negative reading means it wasn't set to zero Flux<String> pipeline = Flux.just(250L, -40L, 1_200L) .doOnNext(g -> System.out.println("emit " + g)) .filter(g -> g > 0).doOnNext(g -> System.out.println(" filter passed " + g)) .map(g -> String.format("%.2f kg", g / 1_000.0)).doOnNext(s -> System.out.println(" map -> " + s)); System.out.println("pipeline built: no line above has printed yet"); pipeline.subscribe(s -> System.out.println(" subscribe " + s)); } }

try.expect: The pipeline built line comes first. Then each weight goes all the way through before the next one is emitted: emit 250, filter passed, map, collect, then emit -40, which stops at the filter, then the third weight. With take(1) only one emit prints: once the collector has its value, the flow is cancelled. The synchronous Flux in the Java twin prints the same order.

sections.h: Move the blocking steps with flowOn, not with withContext around emit
sections.html:
A flow runs in the context of the coroutine that collects it. The context is the small set of settings that travels with a coroutine, the note clipped to the dish from lesson 4 of this track. That includes its dispatcher, the part of the library that picks the thread. The docs call this context preservation, and it means the collector never has to wonder which thread its lambda runs on.

It also rules out the obvious way to move a blocking source to Dispatchers.IO, the bench by the door from lesson 4 of this track. Say the grocer's deliveries come with a note, a small text file with one line per item, such as flour,2000,g. The kitchen reads it with an old reader whose readLine blocks, so the reading belongs on that bench:

Java
// Java equivalent: Reactor has no such rule; subscribeOn moves the source to another scheduler
Flux.<DeliveryLine>generate(sink -> {
        String line = reader.readLine();
        if (line == null) sink.complete(); else sink.next(parseLine(line));
    })
    .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());
Kotlin
// Naive: emit from another context throws IllegalStateException ("Flow invariant is violated")
flow { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit(parseLine(reader.readLine()!!)) } }

// Fixed: flowOn changes the context of everything above it
flow {
    while (true) emit(parseLine(reader.readLine() ?: break))
}.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)

emit must run in the collector's context, and the builder checks every call. It's strict about this, and its error message, "Flow invariant is violated", reads like a court ruling. The reason is in the last section: emit calls the next step's code directly. An emit inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO) would run the collector's lambda on an IO thread that the collector never asked for.

flowOn(dispatcher) is the tool. It changes the context of the part of the chain above it, the upstream, and leaves everything below it, the collector included, where it was. To do that, it runs the upstream in a separate coroutine and puts a small queue between the two halves (lesson 9 of this track calls it a channel). So with flowOn, the reading can run ahead of the collector by up to 64 lines, the default buffer size, instead of exactly one. For a file read that's usually what you want.

FlowOnDemo, in the Try it below, prints the thread for each step. Predict them first:

read   on DefaultDispatcher-worker-1
parse  on DefaultDispatcher-worker-1
format on main
save   on main  flour: 2000
read   on DefaultDispatcher-worker-1
parse  on DefaultDispatcher-worker-1
format on main
save   on main  eggs: 12

read and parse sit above flowOn(Dispatchers.IO), so they ran on a worker thread (IO and Default share one pool, as lesson 4 of this track showed). format and save sit below it, and they stayed on main, the collector's thread.

Reactor's nearest tools are subscribeOn, which moves the source, and publishOn, which moves what follows it; the reactive track covers both. The difference that matters is the subscriber. With Reactor, unless you add a publishOn, the subscriber runs on the scheduler's thread too. With flowOn, the collector always stays in its own context.

So don't reach for flowOn to move the collector. If the collecting side blocks (it writes each line to a file, say), wrap the terminal call instead: withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { flow.collect { writer.write(it) } }.

flowOn moves the steps above it. The collector stays where it is.

The slow part now runs on the bench by the door. The last question is what happens when a step fails.

Run it.

code.title: FlowOnDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOn import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext private fun thread() = Thread.currentThread().name fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { if (args.firstOrNull() == "wrong") { try { flow { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit("flour,2000,g") } // emit from another context }.collect { println("collected $it") } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("IllegalStateException: " + e.message!!.lines().first()) } return@runBlocking } flow { for (line in listOf("flour,2000,g", "eggs,12,pcs")) { Thread.sleep(50) // a blocking read from the delivery note file println("read on ${thread()}") emit(line) } } .map { println("parse on ${thread()}"); parse(it) } .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) // everything above this line runs on IO .map { println("format on ${thread()}"); "${it.first}: ${it.second}" } .collect { println("save on ${thread()} $it") } } private fun parse(line: String): Pair<String, Long> = line.split(",").let { it[0] to it[1].toLong() }

alt.title: FlowOnDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of FlowOnDemo.kt: Reactor's subscribeOn moves the source to another scheduler, // and publishOn moves everything after it. Without a publishOn, the subscriber runs on that // scheduler's thread too, which is the difference from flowOn. package workbench.coroutines.l07; import java.util.List; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; public class FlowOnDemoJava { static String thread() { return Thread.currentThread().getName(); } public static void main(String[] args) { Flux.fromIterable(List.of("flour,2000,g", "eggs,12,pcs")) .doOnNext(line -> { try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } // a blocking file read System.out.println("read on " + thread()); }) .map(line -> { System.out.println("parse on " + thread()); return line.split(","); }) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // the source and the steps above run there .publishOn(Schedulers.single()) // the steps below move to another thread .map(f -> { System.out.println("format on " + thread()); return f[0] + ": " + f[1]; }) .doOnNext(s -> System.out.println("save on " + thread() + " " + s)) .blockLast(); } }

try.expect: read and parse run on a DefaultDispatcher-worker thread, while format and save run on main. After the move, format joins them on the worker, but save stays on main: no flowOn can move the collector. With -Pargs=wrong you get IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated. The Java twin needs subscribeOn for the source and publishOn to move the later steps, which run on single-1.

sections.h: Handle errors from above with catch, and every ending with onCompletion
sections.html:
Flows make a promise called exception transparency. An exception thrown downstream, by a step below or by the collector, belongs to the downstream, and a flow must not catch it and carry on emitting. The error-handling operators are built around that promise.

catch { e -> ... } handles exceptions from the part of the flow above it. It can log, emit a fallback value, or rethrow. Exceptions thrown below it, including inside collect { }, pass straight through to whoever called collect. In the kitchen, catch is the rule for trouble at the stove: if the delivery note is torn halfway, write "aborted" and stop. It has nothing to say about a plate the diner drops.

onCompletion { cause -> } is the flow's finally. It runs once, however the flow ends. cause is null after a normal end, the exception after a failure above or below, and a CancellationException when the collector stopped early, as take and first do. Unlike catch, it handles nothing: the exception carries on after it. Here's the delivery note put away into the pantry:

Java
// Java equivalent: onErrorResume only handles errors from above it; doFinally runs on every exit
deliveryLines(reader)
    .<StockEvent>map(l -> new Stocked(l.item()))
    .doFinally(signal -> System.out.println("delivery ended: " + signal))
    .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just(new Aborted(e.getMessage())))
    .doOnNext(pantry::save)
    .blockLast();
Kotlin
deliveryLines(reader, Dispatchers.IO)                            // may throw IOException
    .map<DeliveryLine, StockEvent> { StockEvent.Stocked(it.item) }
    .onCompletion { cause -> println("delivery ended: $cause") }    // sees every way the flow ends
    .catch { e -> emit(StockEvent.Aborted(e.message ?: "error")) }  // failures above it only
    .collect { pantry.save(it) }                                    // a failure here reaches the caller

CatchDemo, in the Try it below, tears the delivery note after two lines:

collect flour
collect eggs
onCompletion: cause = java.io.IOException: delivery note torn
catch: java.io.IOException: delivery note torn
collect ABORTED
collect returned normally

Now the same chain with the note intact and a full shelf instead, so saving the eggs throws inside the collector (-Pargs=collector):

collect flour
collect eggs
onCompletion: cause = java.lang.IllegalStateException: pantry shelf full
the caller got: java.lang.IllegalStateException: pantry shelf full

catch printed nothing. The failure happened below it, so it went straight to the caller, and onCompletion saw it on the way past.

The classic way to break the promise is a try and catch around emit inside a builder. emit runs the downstream code, so that catch also catches the collector's exceptions, and if it then emits again, the flow throws IllegalStateException ("Flow exception transparency is violated"). That's one of the bugs in this lesson's lab. Use the catch operator instead, which knows where it sits.

Cold flows pay off here once more. retry(3) recovers by collecting the upstream again, and that works only because the recipe can be cooked again from the top.

catch covers the steps above it, never the collector. Put the work that may fail above it.

When you do want a save failure handled, that's the shape the Kotlin docs show: move the save into onEach above the catch, then call collect() with no lambda.

Run the Java twin both ways.

code.title: CatchDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.catch import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.onCompletion import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.io.IOException fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val failIn = args.firstOrNull() ?: "upstream" // or "collector" val lines = flow { emit("flour,2000,g") emit("eggs,12,pcs") if (failIn == "upstream") throw IOException("delivery note torn") emit("butter,250,g") } try { lines .map { it.substringBefore(",") } .onCompletion { cause -> println("onCompletion: cause = $cause") } .catch { e -> println("catch: $e"); emit("ABORTED") } .collect { item -> println("collect $item") if (failIn == "collector" && item == "eggs") throw IllegalStateException("pantry shelf full") } println("collect returned normally") } catch (e: Exception) { println("the caller got: $e") } }

alt.title: CatchDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of CatchDemo.kt: onErrorResume only handles errors from above it, like catch, // and doFinally runs on every way out, like onCompletion. An exception thrown in the subscriber's // own lambda is not an upstream error: no operator above it gets to "handle" it. package workbench.coroutines.l07; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.UncheckedIOException; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; public class CatchDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { String failIn = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "upstream"; // or "collector" Flux<String> lines = Flux.concat( Flux.just("flour,2000,g", "eggs,12,pcs"), failIn.equals("upstream") ? Flux.error(new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("delivery note torn"))) : Flux.just("butter,250,g")); try { lines .map(l -> l.substring(0, l.indexOf(','))) .doFinally(signal -> System.out.println("doFinally: signal = " + signal)) .onErrorResume(e -> { System.out.println("onErrorResume: " + e); return Flux.just("ABORTED"); }) .doOnNext(item -> { System.out.println("consume " + item); if (failIn.equals("collector") && item.equals("eggs")) throw new IllegalStateException("pantry shelf full"); }) .blockLast(); System.out.println("blockLast returned normally"); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("the caller got: " + e); } } }

try.expect: Torn note: flour and eggs are collected, onCompletion prints the IOException, catch prints it and emits ABORTED, which is collected, and collect returns normally. Full shelf: onCompletion prints the IllegalStateException, catch prints nothing, and the caller gets pantry shelf full. The Java twin matches: onErrorResume only handles the upstream error, and doFinally reports onError or cancel.

compare.title: Putting a delivery away: Flux vs Flow

java.title: DeliveryImport.java
java.html: Flux<StockEvent> putAway(LineReader reader) { return Flux.<DeliveryLine>generate(sink -> { // 1. a cold source, pulled on demand String line = reader.readLine(); if (line == null) sink.complete(); else sink.next(parseLine(line)); }) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // 2. the blocking read runs elsewhere .<StockEvent>map(l -> new Stocked(l.item())) .doFinally(signal -> log("delivery ended: " + signal)) // 3. every ending .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just(new Aborted(e.getMessage()))); // 4. upstream errors only }

kotlin.title: DeliveryImport.kt
kotlin.html: fun putAway(reader: LineReader): Flow<StockEvent> = flow { // 1. a cold source, plain step-by-step code while (true) emit(parseLine(reader.readLine() ?: break)) } .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) // 2. the blocking read runs elsewhere .map<DeliveryLine, StockEvent> { StockEvent.Stocked(it.item) } .onCompletion { cause -> log("delivery ended: $cause") } // 3. every ending .catch { e -> emit(StockEvent.Aborted(e.message ?: "error")) } // 4. upstream errors only

compare.note: The shapes line up step for step, and both are cold. The source is where they differ most. Reactor needs a generator callback with an explicit sink, because a Flux source must answer request(n) from its subscribers. A Flow source is an ordinary loop: emit suspends until the collector is ready, so backpressure comes from suspension. Threads differ too. subscribeOn moves the whole chain until a publishOn moves it again, so Reactor subscribers often end up on a scheduler thread. flowOn moves only the upstream, and the collector stays in its own coroutine context. The error operators are nearly identical: catch and onErrorResume both handle only what is above them, and onCompletion and doFinally both run on every ending.

worked.title: Stream a price list to a file instead of loading it

steps.say: A program writes the grocer's whole price list to a file. It loads every item of every page into a list first, then writes. For a catalogue of two million items the program runs out of memory, and nothing at all is written until the last page is in.
steps.code: suspend fun exportPrices(aisle: String, out: Path) { val all = mutableListOf<Item>() var cursor: String? = null do { val page = shop.page(aisle, cursor) all += page.items // every item held in memory cursor = page.nextCursor } while (cursor != null) withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { Files.write(out, all.filter { it.priceCents > 0 }.map(::format)) } }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the same design: collect everything, then write void exportPrices(String aisle, Path out) throws IOException { List<Item> all = new ArrayList<>(); String cursor = null; do { ItemPage page = shop.page(aisle, cursor); all.addAll(page.items()); // every item held in memory cursor = page.nextCursor(); } while (cursor != null); Files.write(out, all.stream().filter(i -> i.priceCents() > 0).map(Export::format).toList()); }

steps.say: Make the source a cold flow. Only one page is in memory at a time, and the next page is fetched only when the writer has caught up.
steps.code: // 1. the source: pages on demand fun aisleItems(aisle: String): Flow<Item> = flow { var cursor: String? = null do { val page = shop.page(aisle, cursor) page.items.forEach { emit(it) } cursor = page.nextCursor } while (cursor != null) }

alt.html: // 1. the source: pages on demand Flux<Item> aisleItems(String aisle) { return shop.page(aisle, null) .expand(p -> p.nextCursor() == null ? Mono.empty() : shop.page(aisle, p.nextCursor())) .flatMapIterable(ItemPage::items); }

steps.say: Build the chain with intermediate operators, and write in the collector. The file write blocks, and it's on the collecting side, so it moves with withContext around the terminal call. flowOn wouldn't help: it never moves the collector.
steps.code: suspend fun exportPrices(aisle: String, out: Path) = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { // 3. the collector's blocking writes run on IO Files.newBufferedWriter(out).use { writer -> aisleItems(aisle) .filter { it.priceCents > 0 } // 2. build: nothing runs yet .map(::format) .collect { line -> writer.write(line); writer.newLine() } // runs it, one line at a time } }

alt.html: void exportPrices(String aisle, Path out) throws IOException { try (BufferedWriter writer = Files.newBufferedWriter(out)) { aisleItems(aisle) .filter(i -> i.priceCents() > 0) // 2. build: nothing runs yet .map(Export::format) .publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // 3. the blocking writes run elsewhere .doOnNext(line -> write(writer, line)) .blockLast(); // runs it } }

steps.say: A half-written price list must not look finished. Delete it when the flow ends with an error. onCompletion sees the cause, and the exception still reaches the caller afterwards, which is what an export should do.
steps.code: aisleItems(aisle) .filter { it.priceCents > 0 } .map(::format) .onCompletion { cause -> if (cause != null) Files.deleteIfExists(out) } // 4. no half files .collect { line -> writer.write(line); writer.newLine() }

alt.html: aisleItems(aisle) .filter(i -> i.priceCents() > 0) .map(Export::format) .publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) .doOnNext(line -> write(writer, line)) .doOnError(e -> deleteQuietly(out)) // 4. no half files .blockLast();

steps.say: Self-check: a caller runs exportPrices(...) inside withTimeout(30.seconds), and the timeout fires halfway. Is the half-written file deleted? (Yes. The timeout cancels the coroutine, so the flow ends with a CancellationException, cause is not null, and onCompletion deletes the file. It runs inside the chain, before use has closed the writer. Linux doesn't mind, but Windows refuses to delete a file that is still open, so a finally around use is the more portable place for the delete.)

lab.title: A grocer's aisle, a delivery reader and a stock report
steps: Meet the code. PantryModel.kt holds the grocer's paged shop (GroceryShop), the old blocking reader for delivery notes (LineReader), one parsed line of a note (DeliveryLine) and the events of putting a delivery away (StockEvent). You write three flows in PantryFlows.kt. Run the tests: seven of eight fail.
Write aisleItems with flow { }: ask for pages starting with cursor null, emit every item, and stop when nextCursor is null. The three aisle tests check that it is lazy, cold and stops early.
Fix deliveryLines: delete the withContext and add .flowOn(io) after the builder.
Rewrite stockReport as a chain: map each line to Stocked, then onCompletion { onDone(it) }, then a catch that emits Aborted(message).
Run the tests until all eight pass.
hints: For aisleItems, a do { ... } while (cursor != null) loop inside flow { } is all you need. emit suspends until the collector is done, so take(3) cancels the loop before the next shop.page call.
map needs to know it produces the sealed type, not Stocked, or catch can't emit Aborted into it. Write .map<DeliveryLine, StockEvent> { ... }.
Put onCompletion above catch: there it sees the upstream exception itself. Below catch it would see null, because catch turned the failure into a normal end.
No try anywhere in stockReport. A try around emit also catches the collector's exceptions, and that breaks exception transparency.

drill.title: A blocking file as a flow, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write fun shoppingList(reader: LineReader): Flow<ListItem> that reads lines with the blocking reader.readLine() (null at the end) on Dispatchers.IO, parses each with parseItem(line), skips items whose quantity is 0, and emits ListItem.INVALID_FILE once if reading or parsing fails.

answer.html: fun shoppingList(reader: LineReader): Flow<ListItem> = flow { while (true) { val line = reader.readLine() ?: break emit(parseItem(line)) } } .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) // the blocking reads, and nothing below .filter { it.quantity != 0L } .catch { emit(ListItem.INVALID_FILE) } // upstream failures only

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent with Reactor Flux<ListItem> shoppingList(LineReader reader) { return Flux.<ListItem>generate(sink -> { String line = reader.readLine(); if (line == null) sink.complete(); else sink.next(parseItem(line)); }) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // the blocking reads .filter(i -> i.quantity() != 0) .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just(ListItem.INVALID_FILE)); // upstream failures only }

recap: A Flow is cold: building it runs nothing, and the flow { } body runs from the top for every collector.
Flows are sequential. emit suspends until the collector is done with the value, which gives backpressure for free, and take stops the producer early.
Intermediate operators (map, filter, onEach, take) build a new flow; terminal operators (collect, toList, first) are suspend functions that run it.
A flow runs in its collector's context. Move the upstream with flowOn(dispatcher); emit inside withContext throws "Flow invariant is violated".
catch handles only exceptions from above it, and onCompletion { cause -> } sees every ending. Never wrap emit in a try.
The limit: a cold flow shares nothing. Every collector repeats every fetch, and nothing here keeps a value for someone who looks later.

explain.prompt: A friend's pantry program ends in .catch { log("import failed", it) }.collect { pantry.save(it) }. When the pantry's database went down, the import failed with an exception instead of logging it, and they think catch is broken. Explain what is going on and how to change the code.
explain.answer: catch only handles exceptions from the part of the chain above it. The save runs in the collect lambda, which is below catch, so when the database failed, the exception went straight to whoever called collect. That's on purpose: flows promise exception transparency, which means a flow never hides the failures of the code downstream of it. If we want the database failure logged the same way, the save has to move above the catch, into onEach, and then we call collect with no lambda: lines.onEach { pantry.save(it) }.catch { log("import failed", it) }.collect(). If the program should stop on a database outage instead, which is probably better, we leave catch for file errors only and let the save failure go up.

deeper.html:
Why does a flow check emit so strictly? Because the operators rely on it. Every operator in the chain runs in one coroutine and assumes that nothing else calls its downstream at the same time. If emit could be called from another coroutine or thread, map and filter would need locks. The checks for context and for exception transparency are what let ordinary step-by-step code be a correct stream operator.

When you need to emit from several coroutines, use channelFlow { }. Its send is safe from any coroutine started inside the builder, because a channel sits between the producers and the collector. callbackFlow { } is the same thing for callback APIs, and it requires awaitClose { unregister() } at the end, or it throws when the block returns. Lesson 9 of this track uses both.

The Flow interface itself is "not stable for inheritance", in the words of its KDoc: write flows with the builders, or extend AbstractFlow if you really need a class. That matters if you are tempted to implement Flow on a class of your own.

buffer(), conflate() and collectLatest change the sequential model on purpose. With a producer that takes 100 ms per item and a collector that takes 300 ms, three items take about (100 + 300) x 3 = 1,200 ms plain, about 100 + 300 x 3 = 1,000 ms with buffer(), and about 700 to 800 ms with conflate(), which skips the middle item. Lesson 9 of this track runs those numbers.

This lesson is the short tour. The Kotlin Flow in depth track, later in the course, builds a flow from two interfaces and a function call, then takes each piece apart: the three checks inside flow { }, flowOn and its buffer, every error operator, and how to test a flow on virtual time.
